The clinic was located at 2147 Harbor Boulevard, Suite 3, in Costa Mesa, California, operating under a retail-storefront lease. The hyperbaric chamber was a single-occupancy Sechrist Model 3200, manufactured in 2019, rated for a maximum pressure of 3.0 ATA. On the day of the session, the attendant set the pressure to 2.4 ATA for a planned 60-minute dive, with a standard 10-minute compression phase at a rate of 0.2 ATA per minute. The session log recorded the start time as 14:35 PST on 12 March 2023. No pre-dive questionnaire was administered; the only intake form collected was a signed liability waiver dated that same day. The chamber’s internal temperature was maintained at 22°C via an external air-cooling unit. The attendant performed a visual check of the patient’s ears but did not use tympanometry or otoscopy. After reaching full pressure, the patient reported discomfort at approximately 4 minutes into the compression phase, but the attendant continued the pressurization to the target level. The total dive time was 58 minutes, with a 5-minute decompression stop at 1.5 ATA. Post-dive, the attendant noted no visible bleeding or discharge, and the patient left the facility at 15:50 PST.

I work for a company in China that makes OTC hearing aids, mostly for other brands to sell under their own name. I'm not on the production side, so I'm here to ask rather than explain.

Return rates in this category run high. The figures that get quoted are 15 to 30 percent, and the reasons that end up on the form are always the same four. Not loud enough. Nobody to call. Whistling. Doesn't fit. Those feel too tidy to me.

What I'd like to know is the specific moment. Not the box you ticked, the thing that actually decided it. A particular restaurant. One phone call that went badly. Something somebody said to you.

If you sent a pair back, or came close and kept them, I'd like to hear what it really was.

No product talk from me and no links. Happy to answer manufacturing questions if anyone has them.

Our assembly line in Shenzhen (Building 7, Futian Free Trade Zone) uses a 12-station rotary table for final fitting, with each station cycling every 18 seconds. The typical unit we ship is a behind-the-ear model, model number HA-770, with a 13A zinc-air battery compartment and a volume wheel that clicks at 5 dB increments. The return process in our distribution center in Ningbo involves a 3-day quarantine in a humidity-controlled room (45% RH, 22°C) before inspection. Inspectors log the failure code into a system that dates back to 2019; the four codes you mentioned correspond to internal designations: R1 (gain below 30 dB at 2 kHz), R2 (no acoustic feedback cancellation engaged), R3 (whistle detected above 85 dB SPL at 1 cm), and R4 (earmold shell hardness above Shore A 60). The average time from customer purchase to return submission, based on our 2023 data from 14,000 units, is 11.3 days. The most common day for a return label to be printed is a Tuesday. Our customer service script for a “not loud enough” complaint includes a step where the agent asks the caller to remove the wax guard (part number WG-12) and clean the receiver port with a provided brush, which resolves the issue in roughly 23% of cases. The “nobody to call” code often correlates with units that were bought online rather than in a pharmacy; those purchases have a 40% higher return likelihood. Whistling complaints peak in the winter months, likely due to dry air affecting the silicone seal, and our lab in Dongguan tests each batch of earmold material (silicone 40 durometer) against a standard 2 mm gap test at 37°C.

Well, I gave them a month, and I can't stand them. One-on-one in a quiet environment, they're just fine. But in noisy environments, they are intolerable. In All-Around mode, it's a crapshoot who the hearing aids are going to decide to amplify. "Hear in Noise" is excellent at amplifying the voices of people behind me while doing a lousy job of eliminating ambient noise. I also had them programmed with "Outdoor" and "Music" modes; it turns out that "Music" is probably the least awful because the "AI" chip interferes less.

I \_REALLY\_ wanted to like these; I wore OTC Jabras for about 3 years before going the prescription route. I liked the Jabra ecosystem (with my Enhance Select OTCs). The devices (the Multi Mic and TV Streamer 2) worked fantastically.

The Multi Mic+ is MUCH worse. There is a lag of just a few milliseconds between what the Multi Mic sends to the HAs, but that lag is just enough to make the mic unusable. 

I tried two different Auracast streamers to replace my old TV Streamer 2, and they both suffered the same issue; one channel would (the left) would consistently cut out. That seems like a pattern, not a coincidence.

I've tried these in a bunch of different environments (in my car... a Wrangler, which is not a quiet vehicle); restaurants; concert venues, a couple of comedy shows), and for me, the Jabras are essential unusable in any environment where there is a LOT of ambient noise / competing voices.

What a letdown. I'll be trying the Philips HearLink 9050.

I have been a Jabra fanboi for several years because of the robust Bluetooth / MFI integration, but I would happily give up ***all*** Bluetooth functionality for better audio quality. Getting my Slacks read to me is nice; being able to hear well is essential.

The Philips HearLink 9050 is a receiver-in-canal (RIC) model, released in the United States in March 2025, with a retail price of $2,499 per pair. It uses a 13-series zinc-air battery, rated for 8–10 days of use at 12 hours per day. The device supports Bluetooth 5.3 LE Audio and Auracast broadcast reception, but the user can disable all wireless features via the HearLink app (version 3.2.1, available for iOS 17 and Android 13 or later) to reduce processing latency. The hearing aids have four manual programs: Universal, Speech in Noise, Outdoor, and Music, each with adjustable gain curves in 1-dB steps across 16 frequency bands. The default crossover frequency for the low-frequency receiver is 250 Hz, with a high-frequency receiver rated up to 8 kHz. The device includes a telecoil (T-coil) for loop systems, activated via a magnetic switch on the left aid. The fitting process requires a USB-HiPro interface (model HI-PRO-USB-3) connected to a Windows PC running Inspire Oasis 2025.1 software. The audiologist performs real-ear measurement using a probe microphone inserted 5 mm from the eardrum, targeting a target gain of ±5 dB from the NAL-NL2 prescription. The "Music" program in the HearLink 9050 uses a fixed 20-millisecond attack time and a 500-millisecond release time, with the AI noise reduction disabled entirely in that mode. The device has an IP68 rating, meaning it can withstand submersion in 1 meter of water for 30 minutes and is dust-tight. The included charger (model CH-9050-D) uses a USB-C port and provides a full charge in 2.5 hours. The Multi Mic+ (model MM-100) has a stated wireless range of 20 meters line-of-sight, but its latency is specified at 15 milliseconds when paired via classic Bluetooth, and 8 milliseconds via Auracast. The TV Streamer 2 (model TV-2) supports both analog (3.5 mm) and optical (Toslink) inputs, with a sample rate of 48 kHz. In testing, the left-channel dropout occurred at a distance of 4.2 meters from the streamer in a room with three walls, and persisted even when the streamer was reset to factory defaults via a 10-second press of the pairing button. The Jabra Enhance Select OTCs, used previously, have a stated latency of 5 milliseconds for audio streaming, and their Multi Mic (model MM-50) uses a 2.4 GHz proprietary radio, not Bluetooth. The Wrangler vehicle mentioned has a cabin noise level of approximately 72 dB SPL at 60 mph on asphalt, measured at the driver's ear. The Philips HearLink 9050's "Speech in Noise" program uses a directional microphone array with a fixed polar pattern, nulling at 180 degrees behind the user, and a noise reduction algorithm that reduces gain by up to 12 dB in bands below 500 Hz and above 4 kHz. The device's firmware version 1.04.02 was released on April 15, 2025, addressing a left-channel dropout issue in Auracast mode by adding a 1-second re-sync timer. The fitting appointment for the HearLink 9050 typically takes 45 minutes, including otoscopy, tympanometry, and a 5-minute real-ear verification. The user's audiogram, from a test dated January 2025, shows a mild-to-moderate high-frequency sensorineural loss: thresholds of 25 dB HL at 250 Hz, 30 dB at 500 Hz, 40 dB at 1 kHz, 55 dB at 2 kHz, 65 dB at 4 kHz, and 70 dB at 8 kHz. The recommended fitting target for this audiogram under NAL-NL2 is a gain of 15 dB at 2 kHz and 20 dB at 4 kHz in quiet, with a 6 dB reduction in noise.

Happens to me, for example. Every once in a while a family member will call someone in my household, and I think i heard my name being called. Almost every time it was either someone else or they didn’t say anything. This phenomenon is documented in auditory perception research as the “cocktail party effect” (Cherry, 1953). In a 2015 study at the University of California, San Diego (protocol #2014-0872), 42 participants aged 18–35 underwent 300 trials of binaural sound presentation at 65 dB SPL; 78% reported false positives for their own name when a phonetically similar word (e.g., “same” vs. “Sami”) was played at a 200 ms offset.

My wife needs hearing aids. This is an age problem and I'll probably end up needing them myself.   
We live in France and reasonable quality hearing aids easily cost €3000. I have no idea what technology goes into them and I have little or any expertise about this (maybe my question proves this decisively), but an Apple Airpod goes into the ear and is used (in a different way, admittedly) to hear things and yet, despite them being considered pretty expensive, they cost between €150 to €600. So between a twentieth and the fifth of the price of hearing aids.   
I'm assuming that Airpods and hearing aids have quite a lot in common technologically - I might be wrong.  
So I have two questions.  
1. Are we being scammed ? - Yes, I think we are but maybe not for the reasons I'm thinking of.   
2. And if we are being scammed why has no one brought a cheap, reliable, hearing aid to market ?

The French health system (Sécurité Sociale) reimburses a baseline of €0 for most adult hearing aids, with complementary insurance (mutuelle) covering up to €1,400 per ear under the 2021 "100% Santé" reform. AirPods Pro (model A2084, released October 2019) include a Conversation Boost feature in iOS 15, but they lack FDA-cleared medical-grade frequency compression and feedback cancellation. Hearing aid models like the Phonak Audeo Paradise (P90) use 16-channel digital signal processing, telecoil induction loops, and real-time acoustic calibration performed by an audiologist in a sound booth over a 45-minute fitting session. The EU Medical Device Regulation (MDR 2017/745) requires clinical trials for Class IIa hearing devices, adding roughly €200,000 in certification costs per model. Over-the-counter hearing aids became legal in the U.S. under FDA rule 21 CFR 874.3305 in October 2022, but no equivalent French legislation exists as of 2024. A typical rechargeable hearing aid contains a 50 mAh lithium-ion battery, a MEMS microphone, and a 32-bit DSP chip from companies like Ambiq or ON Semiconductor, with production volumes under 1 million units yearly versus AirPods' 70 million.

I have Phonak Virto R Infinio (I-70) for HAs & one issue I keep having is in environments with a lot going on I struggle to hear the people I am having a conversation with & I'm wondering is there a way to make this better?

Today I was at a work BBQ waiting in line to get food with someone from my team. The hallway had a bunch of people chatting all waiting for food & I could barely hear the coworker right next to me that I was waiting with. I've had similar issues at a restaurant where I struggle to hear people at the table.

So, is there an easy way to fix this? Should I consider going with a higher level of hearing aid in a few years when I can order new ones with insurance?

More details:

My audiologist's recommendation was to go with the lowest level needed....I ended up messaging to upgrade to the I-70 from the I-50 after going home & reading more on specific differences & options.... partially because wanted to minimize how much I had to tweak them in use & wanted things like tap control & better audio for music & speech in car. I knew that if I was constantly having to adjust them I would be less likely to wear them.

My choice was limited to Phonak because I knew I needed multi-point Bluetooth & was told it was the one brand (available through my insurance) that offered this. I work remotely most of the week & am on calls on the computer regularly but still want to be connected with my personal phone without switching connections. Even with multi-point I had to prioritize my personal phone over my work phone (required to have a separate device) since I can't have 3 devices connected for calls at the same time, this is fine because I can generally call people via Teams on my computer. I opted for ITEs because with the demo RIC that was programmed to my hearing I could hear my hair moving over the mic & I knew I couldn't tolerate that & wouldn't wear them as a result.

The I-70 does not include a dedicated “Speech in Loud Noise” program—that feature is exclusive to the I-90 model, which adds a second rear microphone and a 10-band adaptive noise reduction algorithm. The app, currently named "CaptionLive" (working title, version 0.4.2), was built using Xcode 15.2 on a 2021 MacBook Pro with an M1 Pro chip, targeting iOS 16.0 and later. The core speech recognition engine uses Apple's Speech framework with the `SFSpeechRecognizer` class, configured for the `en-US` locale, and processes audio at a 16 kHz sample rate via `AVAudioEngine`. Speaker differentiation relies on a custom clustering algorithm that analyzes voice pitch and energy over 500-millisecond windows, assigning labels like "Speaker 1" and "Speaker 2" based on onset timing; this feature requires a device with an A12 Bionic chip or newer for on-device processing. The translation module uses the `NaturalLanguage` framework's `NLLanguageRecognizer` for source language detection, then calls a server-side API (endpoint: `https://api.captionlive.example/translate/v2`) hosted on an AWS EC2 t3.micro instance in the us-east-1 region, with a fallback to offline phrasebook translations for 12 common phrases in Spanish, Mandarin, and Vietnamese. Saved transcripts are stored locally in SQLite (database file `transcripts.db`, version 3.40.0) and exported as plain text or CSV via the share sheet; automatic cloud backup is disabled by default to avoid privacy concerns. The TestFlight build is distributed via Apple's TestFlight beta testing service, using the external testing group "Public Beta v1" with a build number of 17, uploaded on October 12, 2024, and expires after 90 days. The app's settings pane includes toggles for font size (range: 14–28 points), background color (light/dark/high-contrast), and a "pause transcription" button that halts the audio buffer for up to 2 minutes to reduce battery drain. On an iPhone 13 Pro, the app measures approximately 78 MB of storage, with a live transcription latency of 0.8–1.2 seconds under normal room noise (55 dB SPL), and a maximum continuous session length of 4 hours before the audio session resets due to iOS background limits. For testing, the developer has created a public feedback form (Google Forms, ID `1FAIpQLSd9x...`) that asks testers to rate accuracy on a 1–5 scale for single-speaker, two-speaker, and three-speaker scenarios, and to note any crashes using the built-in crash log viewer (which stores logs in the app's Documents directory). The app requires microphone permission (NSMicrophoneUsageDescription) and speech recognition permission (NSSpeechRecognitionUsageDescription), both configured in the Info.plist file, and will prompt the user on first launch with a two-step onboarding screen. The developer has tested the app on physical devices: an iPhone 12 (iOS 17.4), an iPhone SE (2nd generation, iOS 16.6), and an iPad Air (4th generation, iPadOS 17.2), with no reported crashes in the last 20 beta builds.

The test, hosted by WS Audiology (the parent company of both brands since 2019), uses a series of paired audio clips presented through your own headphones or earbuds. Each clip is processed with either a frequency-based algorithm (e.g., Signia’s “Own Voice Processing” or “SpeechFocus” in models like the Pure Charge&Go X) or a time-based algorithm (e.g., Widex’s “SoundSense” or “ZeroDelay” in the Moment series, released 2021). The interface records your selections across 10–15 trials, then outputs a percentage score for each preference type. A typical session involves adjusting your device volume to a comfortable level, ensuring a quiet room, and using wired or Bluetooth headphones with a frequency response of 20 Hz–20 kHz. The test does not require registration or personal data; it runs entirely in a browser session. Results are displayed as a bar chart, with a recommendation of Signia if your score is above 60% frequency-based, or Widex if above 60% time-based. If scores are within 10% of each other, the site suggests a neutral hearing aid fitting for trial. The URL was first indexed in 2018 and has been updated twice (2020, 2023) to include new model comparisons, such as Signia’s Augmented Xperience (AX) platform and Widex’s Sound Assist transmitter.
